questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Concept of Planning' refers to.
questions.a: The managerial function of settling in advance both the targets to be pursued and the route to reach them, so that the distance between an organisation's present position and its desired one is crossed deliberately.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Concept of Planning'.
questions.a: Planning handles ends and means together: it fixes objectives for a period, drafts alternative courses of action, and picks the best among them.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Concept of Planning' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 1.1 (source: lebs104.txt lines 90-159 (Concept; deciding in advance; ends and means))

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Importance of Planning' refers to.
questions.a: The benefits the function delivers: it gives every unit a common direction, lowers the danger from uncertainty through forecasts, trims duplicated and useless work, turns fresh ideas into concrete plans, sharpens decision making, and supplies the yardsticks that controlling later measures against.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Importance of Planning'.
questions.a: Six benefits -- direction, less uncertainty, less overlapping, innovation, better decisions, standards for controlling; planning is the prerequisite of controlling.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Importance of Planning' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 2.1 (source: lebs104.txt lines 160-315 (Importance i to vi))

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Features of Planning' refers to.
questions.a: Seven marks of the function: it exists to reach objectives, comes before every other managerial function, runs at all levels and departments, never stops, peers into the future through forecasting, demands a choice among alternatives, and stays an intellectual exercise rather than physical doing.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Features of Planning'.
questions.a: Primacy means all other functions operate inside the frame the plan sets; pervasiveness means top plans the whole firm, middle plans departments, supervisors plan daily operations.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Features of Planning' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 3.1 (source: lebs104.txt lines 316-503 (Features i to vii))

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Limitations of Planning' refers to.
questions.a: The drawbacks of the function: fixed plans can turn rigid when circumstances move, a shifting environment defeats forecasts, lower levels lose their creative voice, preparing plans costs heavy money and time, and even an old winning plan offers no promise of repeating its success.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Limitations of Planning'.
questions.a: Six limitations -- rigidity, dynamic environment, reduced creativity, huge cost, time consumption, no guarantee of success.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Limitations of Planning' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 4.1 (source: lebs104.txt lines 504-643 (Limitations i to vi))

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Steps in the Planning Process' refers to.
questions.a: Seven ordered steps: fix the objectives, build the premises or assumptions about the future, list every possible course of action, weigh each against feasibility and consequence, choose the best one, put it into action, and monitor how it runs.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Steps in the Planning Process'.
questions.a: The real decision point arrives at selecting an alternative; a sales manager drafting option lists is performing the identifying-alternatives step.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Steps in the Planning Process' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 5.1 (source: lebs104.txt lines 644-936 (Planning Process i to vii))

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Single-use versus Standing Plans' refers to.
questions.a: Two families of operational plans: single-use plans serve one non-repeating event or project and cover budgets, programmes and projects, while standing plans handle activities that recur regularly and cover policies, procedures, methods and rules.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Single-use versus Standing Plans'.
questions.a: The test is repetition -- a seminar next month needs a single-use plan; e-payment for all daily bills is a standing rule.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Single-use versus Standing Plans' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 6.1 (source: lebs104.txt lines 937-1009 (Single-use and standing plans, their contents))

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Objectives and Strategy' refers to.
questions.a: Objectives are the end results an organisation wants to reach, stated measurably and within a time limit; strategy is the comprehensive top-level plan that combines long-run objectives, the chosen course of action, and the allocation of resources needed, all read against the environment and competition.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Objectives and Strategy'.
questions.a: Strategy has three dimensions -- determine long-term objectives, adopt a course of action, allocate resources; objectives are the end points everything else serves.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Objectives and Strategy' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 6.2 (source: lebs104.txt lines 1035-1136 (Objectives; Strategy and its three dimensions))

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Policy, Procedure, Method and Rule' refers to.
questions.a: The ladder of standing plans: a policy is a general statement that channels thinking and leaves room for discretion, a procedure spells the chronological steps inside that policy, a method prescribes how one step of a procedure is performed, and a rule is a blunt specific command admitting no discretion at all.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Policy, Procedure, Method and Rule'.
questions.a: Discretion shrinks down the ladder -- widest under policy, narrow at procedure, technical at method, zero at rule.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Policy, Procedure, Method and Rule' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 6.3 (source: lebs104.txt lines 1137-1248 (Policy, Procedure, Method, Rule))

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Programme and Budget as Plans' refers to.
questions.a: A programme is the detailed project statement that bundles objectives, policies, procedures, rules, tasks, resources and the money allotted, while a budget is a plan expressed purely in numbers so that actual figures can later be compared with expected ones and corrected.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Programme and Budget as Plans'.
questions.a: A budget quantifies a plan and doubles as a control device -- deviations of actual from budgeted figures stand out immediately.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Programme and Budget as Plans' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 6.4 (source: lebs104.txt lines 1249-1295 (Programme; Budget as a numerical plan and control device))

questions.q: Compute the net cash position from the quarter's expected collections and payments. Use the method 'Cash Budget -- Surplus or Deficiency'. Work with: cash_inflows = 240, cash_outflows = 18. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of net_cash_position.
questions.a: 222 rupees

questions.q: How much spare cash or shortfall results when receipts of {cash_inflows} meet payments of {cash_outflows}? Use the method 'Cash Budget -- Surplus or Deficiency'. Work with: cash_inflows = 80, cash_outflows = 45. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of net_cash_position.
questions.a: 35 rupees

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Cash Budget -- Surplus or Deficiency' refers to.
questions.a: A period statement of the cash a firm expects to collect and the cash it expects to pay; netting the two reveals whether the firm will sit on spare cash or fall short and need to arrange funds.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Cash Budget -- Surplus or Deficiency'.
questions.a: Collections below payments mean a deficiency to finance; spare cash sitting idle earns almost nothing, so the firm sizes its cash need with care.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Cash Budget -- Surplus or Deficiency', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: net_cash_position = cash_inflows - cash_outflows
